citations.quote: Choose $t\in E$ such that $(t,\alpha)\ne0$ for every root. Put $\Phi^+=\{\alpha:(t,\alpha)>0\}$ and $\Phi^-=-\Phi^+$. A positive root is **simple** if it is not the sum of two positive roots. The following positive-root lemma proves that the simple roots form a basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ and that the simple reflections $s_i=s_{\alpha_i}$ generate $W$; no such assertion is assumed by this definition. Once proved, let $\ell(w)$ be the least number of simple reflections in a word for $w$ and let $\operatorname{Inv}(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi^+:w\alpha\in\Phi^-\}$. A word is reduced if its length equals $\ell(w)$.

For the preceding finite reduced crystallographic root system, regular vectors $t$ exist, $W$ is finite, and the simple positive roots are a basis of $E$. Every root has integral coordinates in this basis of one sign. Each $s_i$ permutes $\Phi^+\setminus\{\alpha_i\}$ and sends $\alpha_i$ to $-\alpha_i$. The simple reflections generate $W$, and every root is the image of a simple root under their group. The simple coroots similarly form an integral basis of the coroot group, and $P$ is the lattice generated by their dual basis; $W$ preserves $Q,Q^\vee,P$. All assertions are choice-free, including rank zero.

Every $W$-orbit in $E$ has exactly one point in $\overline{\mathcal C}$. For $\eta\in\overline{\mathcal C}$, its stabilizer is generated by those simple reflections $s_i$ with $(\eta,\alpha_i)=0$. The group acts simply transitively on open chambers. There is a unique longest element $w_0$, characterized by $w_0\Phi^+=\Phi^-$; it has length $|\Phi^+|$ and satisfies $w_0^2=1$. In particular every weight orbit has a unique dominant weight. These assertions include rank zero and singular wall points, without AC.

Let $\Phi\subseteq E$ be a reduced crystallographic root system in the real
inner product space $E$ ([[def-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]).
For $\alpha\in\Phi$ put
$$\alpha^{\vee}=\frac{2\alpha}{(\alpha,\alpha)}\in E .$$
The vector $\alpha^\vee$ is the **coroot** of $\alpha$, and the set
$$\Phi^{\vee}=\{\alpha^{\vee}:\alpha\in\Phi\}$$
is the **dual root system**.

Let $\Phi\subseteq E$ be a reduced crystallographic root system with base
$\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$
([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]],
[[thm-simple-roots-form-a-basis-and-every-root-has-one-sign-of-integral-coordinates]])
and coroots $\alpha^{\vee}=2\alpha/(\alpha,\alpha)\in E$
([[def-coroot-and-dual-root-system]]). The **root lattice**, **coroot
lattice**, **weight lattice**, and **coweight lattice** are
$$Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb Z\alpha_i,\qquad Q^{\vee}=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha^{\vee}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb Z\alpha_i^{\vee},$$
$$P=\{\lambda\in E:(\lambda,\alpha^{\vee})\in\mathbb Z\text{ for all }\alpha\in\Phi\},\qquad P^{\vee}=\{\mu\in E:(\alpha,\mu)\in\mathbb Z\text{ for all }\alpha\in\Phi\}.$$
All four sets are additive subgroups of $E$, since the integrality conditions
are preserved by addition and negation; they are free abelian groups of rank
$r$, for $Q$ and $Q^{\vee}$ because the simple roots and the simple coroots
are bases of $E$, and for $P$ and $P^{\vee}$ because the simple coroots are
again a basis so the dual lattice is generated by the dual basis. The chain
$$Q\subseteq P,\qquad Q^{\vee}\subseteq P^{\vee}$$
holds because the Cartan integers $\langle\alpha,\beta^{\vee}\rangle=2(\alpha,\beta)/(\beta,\beta)$
are integers for all roots
([[def-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]).

**(4) Comparison.** The finite root-system types are the standard crystallographic types $A_n,B_n,C_n,D_n,E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,G_2$ (with the low-rank identifications in [[thm-classification-of-irreducible-reduced-crystallographic-root-systems]]). In that root-system normalization, $W_a=Q^\vee\rtimes W$ from [[lem-cg-affine-reflection-identities-and-local-finiteness]] is the standard affine Weyl group. This does not identify it with an untwisted Kac–Moody loop realization, and it does not assert that the extended group $P^\vee\rtimes W$ is a Coxeter group with the same simple system. No axiom of choice is used.

For the simple reflections of a finite reduced crystallographic root system, word length equals inversion length: $\ell(w)=|\operatorname{Inv}(w)|$. If a root reflection $t$ satisfies $\ell(tw)<\ell(w)$, every reduced word for $w$ loses exactly one letter to give $tw$. Every nonreduced word admits deletion of two letters without changing its group element.

For the preceding finite reduced crystallographic root system, regular vectors $t$ exist, $W$ is finite, and the simple positive roots are a basis of $E$. Suppose $q=\kappa-w\kappa\in Q$. Since $q$ is real,
$b=wb$. Thus $w\in W_b$. Each reflection generating $W_b$ fixes the
orthogonal complement of its root, so $a-wa\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb
R}\Phi_b$; also $q=a-wa$, hence $q\in Q_b$ by [F1]–[F2]. The affine
transformation $t_qw$ of the dual affine Weyl group $Q_b\rtimes W_b$ fixes
the orthogonal projection $a_b$ of $a$ to
$E_b=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi_b$.

In any locally finite affine root-wall arrangement, the stabilizer of a
point $a_b$ is generated by the reflections in walls through that point. To
see this, choose a ball about $a_b$ meeting no wall not containing $a_b$.
Inside it, the finitely many hyperplanes through $a_b$ cut local chambers;
generic line segments join any two local chambers by crossing one wall at a
time and avoiding their codimension-two intersections. The corresponding
wall reflections therefore act transitively on the local chambers. If an
affine Weyl element fixes $a_b$, choose a local chamber $C$ and a product $h$
of these reflections carrying $C$ to its image. Then $h^{-1}g$ preserves the
global alcove containing $C$, so it is the identity by the simple transitivity
in [F3]. Hence $g=h$. Apply this to $g=t_qw$ from [step 1.1]. Every generating
wall has a root $\alpha\in\Phi_b$ and
$\langle a,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$; since $b$ is perpendicular to
$\alpha$, also $\langle\kappa,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$. Taking finite
parts shows that $w$ belongs to the subgroup $W_{\mathrm{int}}$ generated by
the reflections $s_\alpha$ for roots with integral $\kappa$-pairing.

The set $\Phi_{\mathrm{int}}=\{\alpha\in\Phi:
\langle\kappa,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z\}$ is stable under its root
reflections: if $m=\langle\kappa,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ and
$\beta\in\Phi_{\mathrm{int}}$, then
$$\langle\kappa,(s_\alpha\beta)^\vee\rangle
=\langle s_\alpha\kappa,\beta^\vee\rangle
=\langle\kappa,\beta^\vee\rangle-m\langle\alpha,\beta^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z,$$
using crystallographic integrality. It is therefore a finite root system in its
span, with positive system $\Phi_{\mathrm{int}}\cap\Phi^+$. For every
$\alpha\in\Phi_{\mathrm{int}}\cap\Phi^+$, antidominance makes the integer
$\langle\kappa,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ nonpositive. If
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_m}$ is reduced in $W_{\mathrm{int}}$, telescoping gives
$$\kappa-w\kappa=\sum_{j=1}^m\langle\kappa,\alpha_{i_j}^\vee\rangle
s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_{j-1}}\alpha_{i_j}.$$
Every prefix root is positive in $\Phi_{\mathrm{int}}$ by [F4], so every term
lies in the negative cone generated by positive roots of $\Phi_{\mathrm{int}}$,
which is contained in $-Q_+$. Thus $q\in-Q_+$.

Combining [step 1.1] and [step 3.1], an assumed
$q\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$ also lies in $-Q_+$, contradicting [F1]. This
proves the antidominant assertion. If $\kappa$ is regular, every integral
root pairing in [step 3.1] is strictly negative. For any nonidentity
$w\in W_{\mathrm{int}}$, its reduced word has at least one term, and each
term is a strictly negative multiple of a positive root; the sum is nonzero
because $Q_+$ is pointed. Hence $q=0$ forces $w=1$, proving the regular
assertion.

$i_{x*}I_x$ has sections $I_x$ on opens containing $x$ and zero on opens not

natural bijection
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr A}(N,i_{x*}I_x)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr A_x}(N_x,I_x)$$

quasi-compact separated scheme ([[def-separated-morphism-schemes]]), let
$U_0,\dots,U_r$ be a finite affine open cover of $X$ and let $\mathcal F$ be a
quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module
([[def-quasi-coherent-module-scheme]]). Then every intersection of one or more
members of this cover is affine, and, writing $C^\bullet(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)$
for the ordered Čech cochain complex of the cover in the given order
([[def-cech-cochain-complex-open-cover]]), the canonical comparison map
$$\check H^q(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow H^q(X,\mathcal F)$$
of the ordered Čech cohomology ([[def-cech-cohomology-open-cover]]) with sheaf
cohomology ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]) is an isomorphism
for every $q\ge0$. The empty scheme is included: its cover may have no
members or any finite number of empty members, and all cochain and cohomology
groups are zero, so the comparison is the unique map $0\to0$. An empty
index set is allowed in this case; $r=0$ gives a one-member cover.

Let $X$ be a scheme. An $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal L$ is **invertible** if
it is locally free of rank $1$
([[def-locally-free-sheaf-finite-rank]]): every point $x\in X$ has an open
neighbourhood $U$ with
$$\mathcal L|_U\;\cong\;\mathcal O_U.$$
Equivalently, $X$ is covered by open sets $U$ on which $\mathcal L|_U$ admits a
generator, that is, a section $s\in\mathcal L(U)$ such that the morphism
$\mathcal O_U\to\mathcal L|_U$, $a\mapsto a\cdot s|_U$, is an isomorphism. The
structure sheaf $\mathcal O_X$ is invertible.

The Cech complex for $U_0,U_1$ has
$$C^0=\mathbb C[z]e_0\oplus\mathbb C[w]e_1,\qquad
C^1=\mathbb C[z,z^{-1}]e_0,$$
with differential
$(f_0,f_1)\mapsto z^d f_1(1/z)-f_0(z)$. Its kernel consists of polynomials
$f_0(z)$ that also lie in $z^d\mathbb C[z^{-1}]$. If $d\ge0$, these are
exactly the span of $1,z,\ldots,z^d$; if $d<0$, the exponent ranges
$\{0,1,\ldots\}$ and $\{d,d-1,\ldots\}$ are disjoint, so the kernel is
zero. This proves the assertion for $H^0$.

The degree-one cohomology is the Laurent-polynomial quotient
$$\mathbb C[z,z^{-1}]/\bigl(\mathbb C[z]+z^d\mathbb C[z^{-1}]\bigr).$$
The first summand spans exponents $n\ge0$ and the second spans $n\le d$.
If $d\ge-1$, these ranges cover every integer, so the quotient is zero. If
$d\le-2$, the missing exponents are exactly
$d+1,d+2,\ldots,-1$, which gives the stated basis and dimension
$-d-1$. The Cech complex has no degree above one, so $H^q=0$ for $q\ge2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and Weyl group $W$,
and let $p_1,\dots,p_r$ be homogeneous basic generators of $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$
of degrees $d_1,\dots,d_r$, corresponding by Chevalley restriction to basic Weyl
invariants ([[thm-symmetric-invariants-restrict-to-weyl-invariants]],
[[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]]). Put
$$A=S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r).$$ Then $A$ is a reduced integral domain of
dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r=2|\Phi^+|$, with Hilbert series
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(A,t)=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{d_i})}{(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}},$$
and for every central character $\chi:Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\mathbb C$ the PBW
associated graded of $U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ is canonically
isomorphic to $A$.

**Maximal torus, roots, positive roots.** Fix a maximal torus $T\subseteq G$,
that is, a closed subgroup isomorphic to a product of copies of
$\mathbb G_m$ which is maximal for this property. Its Lie algebra
$\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}T$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak g$ and
$\mathfrak g$ decomposes as
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha$
with $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ the root space of the root $\alpha\in\mathfrak h^*$
in the sense of [[def-root-and-root-space-relative-to-a-cartan-subalgebra]].
We write $\Phi=\Phi(G,T)\subseteq\mathfrak h^*$ for this root set, a reduced
crystallographic root system in the real span of $\Phi$, and we fix once and
for all a positive system $\Phi^+$ with simple roots $\Delta$, in the sense of
[[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]]. Define the nilpotent Lie
subalgebras
$$\mathfrak n^\pm=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi^\pm}\mathfrak g_\alpha,\qquad \mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+.$$
Here $\mathfrak b$ is the Borel subalgebra of
[[def-positive-and-negative-nilpotent-subalgebras-and-borel-subalgebra]].

(iii) Repeating the construction with the negative roots produces the closed
connected unipotent subgroup $U^-$ with $\operatorname{Lie}U^-=\mathfrak n^-$
and the closed connected solvable subgroup
$B^-=T\cdot U^-=T\ltimes U^-$ with $\operatorname{Lie}B^-=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^-$.

On a principal $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ string with highest weight $2m>0$,
$\operatorname{ad}h$ has weights $-2m,-2m+2,\ldots,2m$. For every $j\ge1$,
if weight $2j$ occurs then weight $2j-2$ occurs, and the raising operator
$\operatorname{ad}e$ maps the latter one-dimensional weight space onto the
former. Summing over the strings in [F1] gives
$$[e,\mathfrak n^+_j]=\mathfrak n^+_{j+1}\qquad(j\ge1),$$
with zero spaces understood above the maximal root height.

Let $x\in\mathfrak n^+$ have nonzero simple coefficients. The map
$T\to(\mathbb C^\times)^r$, $t\mapsto(\alpha_i(t))_i$, is an isogeny:
its character-lattice map has image the full-rank root lattice. An isogeny of
complex tori is surjective on complex points, so conjugation by one $t\in T$
sets all simple coefficients of $x$ to $1$. Now suppose heights below $j+1$
already agree with those of $e$. Their height-$(j+1)$ difference lies in
$\mathfrak n^+_{j+1}$; by [step 1.1] choose $u_j\in\mathfrak n^+_j$ whose
bracket with $e$ cancels that difference. The finite exponential
$\exp(\operatorname{ad}u_j)$ changes no height at most $j$ and changes height
$j+1$ by $[u_j,e]$; all its higher commutators have height at least $j+2$.
Induction over the finitely many root heights conjugates $x$ to $e$ by $U$.

Conversely, conjugation by $T$ scales each simple-root coefficient by a
nonzero scalar. For $u\in U$, every commutator in
$\exp(\operatorname{ad}u)e-e$ has height at least two, because $u$ has
positive height and $e$ has height one. Thus $U$ fixes the simple-root
coefficients, and $B=TU$ preserves their nonvanishing. The inclusion in the
right side and the reverse inclusion from step 1.2 prove the equality. The
rank-zero case has $\mathfrak n^+=0$, $e=0$ and both sides are the singleton
$\{0\}$.

The orbit map $G\to N$, $g\mapsto\operatorname{Ad}(g)e$, has irreducible
image closure. By [F1] its image has dimension
$\dim\mathfrak g-\dim Z_{\mathfrak g}(e)=2|\Phi^+|=\dim N$; by [F5] the
constructible image is dense and therefore contains a nonempty open subset
of the irreducible variety $N$. The orbit is $G$-stable, so its translates
of this open subset cover the orbit; consequently $G\cdot e$ is open in $N$.

If $y\in N\setminus G\cdot e$, conjugate it into $\mathfrak n^+$ by
[F1]. At least one simple-root coefficient must vanish by [F2]. For each
simple $\alpha_i$, let $\mathfrak n_i$ be the sum of all positive root
spaces except $\mathfrak g_{\alpha_i}$; it is the nilradical of
$P_{\alpha_i}$ and has dimension $|\Phi^+|-1$. Therefore
$N\setminus G\cdot e$ is contained in the finite union of the images of
$$G\times^{P_{\alpha_i}}\mathfrak n_i\longrightarrow N.$$
Each source has dimension
$(|\Phi^+|-1)+(|\Phi^+|-1)=2|\Phi^+|-2$ by [F4]. Hence the complement of
the open regular orbit has codimension at least two. The Jacobian rank at $e$
is full by the proof of [F1]; $G$-equivariance makes every point of $G\cdot e$
regular. Thus $N$ is regular in codimension one. Since it is an integral
complete intersection, [F6] gives normality.

The Springer map is
$$\mu:G\times^B\mathfrak n^+\longrightarrow N,\qquad[g,x]\longmapsto\operatorname{Ad}(g)x.$$
Its graph is the incidence subvariety
$$\{(gB,y)\in X\times N:y\in\operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak n^+\},$$
which is closed because the spaces $\operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak n^+$ form
a vector subbundle of $X\times\mathfrak g$. The projection $X\times N\to N$
is projective by [F4], so $\mu$ is proper by the projective-morphism theorem
included in [F4]. Surjectivity follows from the last clause of [F1].

The fiber over $e$ is a single point. Indeed, if $e\in\operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak n^+$,
write $g=b_1n_wb_2$ by [F3]. The element $x=\operatorname{Ad}(b_1^{-1})e$
still has every simple coefficient nonzero by [F2]. Since
$\operatorname{Ad}(n_w^{-1})x\in\mathfrak n^+$, each nonzero simple-root
component of $x$ must map to a positive root space; distinct root spaces
cannot cancel. Therefore $w^{-1}$ sends every positive simple root to a
positive root, so $w=1$ by [F3], and $gB=B$. Equivariance gives a singleton
fiber over every point of $G\cdot e$. The map is generically finite of
geometric degree one over this open orbit; generic smoothness in [F5]
ensures the generic fiber is reduced in characteristic zero, hence the
function-field degree is one. Thus $\mu$ is birational.

Let $R=\mathbb C[N]$ and $S=\Gamma(T^*X,\mathcal O)$. Properness makes
$S=\Gamma(N,\mu_*\mathcal O_{T^*X})$ a finite $R$-algebra by [F7].
Birationality embeds $S$ in $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and contains $R$.
Every element of a finite $R$-algebra is integral over $R$ by the determinant
trick. Since $R$ is integrally closed by step 2.1, $S=R$. This proves the
Springer-functions isomorphism without inferring regularity of a rational
function from connected fibers.

Let $\phi_\kappa:U(\mathfrak g)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal D_\kappa)$ be the
filtered map from the infinitesimal action. Its central character is exactly
$\chi_\kappa$. At $eB$, the right-Verma fiber of the action-algebroid
filtration is induced from the isotropy character on the source line
$\mathcal O_X(\kappa+\rho)^*$ tensored with the canonical line
$\omega_X$. By [F4] the latter character is $2\rho$, so this inducing
character is $-(\kappa+\rho)+2\rho=\rho-\kappa$. Converting the right action
to a left action by the principal antiautomorphism $x\mapsto-x$ gives the
highest weight $\kappa-\rho$. The central scalar is therefore
$\operatorname{pr}(z)(\kappa-\rho)=\chi_\kappa(z)$ by [F5]. The calculation
is $G$-equivariant, so it holds at every closed point of $X$.

Fix an order bound $m$. The space $U(\mathfrak g)_{\le m}$ is
finite-dimensional by PBW, and $F_m\mathcal D_\kappa$ is locally free of
finite rank by [F1]. For $z\in\ker\chi_\kappa$, the multiplication map
$\mathcal O_X\otimes U(\mathfrak g)_{\le m}\to F_{m+d(z)}\mathcal D_\kappa$
given by $u\mapsto\phi_\kappa(u(z-\chi_\kappa(z)))$ is zero on every closed
fiber by step 1.1. In local frames this is a finite matrix of regular
functions vanishing at every closed point; $X$ is reduced and of finite type
over $\mathbb C$, so each entry is zero. Thus $\phi_\kappa$ kills the whole
two-sided central ideal and factors through a filtered map
$\bar\phi_\kappa:A_\kappa\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal D_\kappa)$. This finite-rank
argument does not apply Nakayama to an infinitely generated module.

The associated-graded map fits into
$$\mathbb C[N]\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}A_\kappa
\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}\Gamma(X,\mathcal D_\kappa)
\hookrightarrow\Gamma(X,\operatorname{gr}\mathcal D_\kappa)
=\Gamma(T^*X,\mathcal O).$$
The last inclusion follows by applying the left-exact functor $\Gamma$ to
each order-filtration sequence. The composite is pullback by the Springer
moment map: for $x\in\mathfrak g$, its linear function on $N$ pulls back to
the principal symbol of the vector field $x_X$, namely
$\xi\mapsto\xi(x_X)$ on $T^*X$. Linear functions generate $\mathbb C[N]$ as
a quotient of $S(\mathfrak g)$, so the two algebra maps agree on all
generators. By [F3] the composite is an isomorphism.

map is injective, both intermediate associated-graded maps are isomorphisms.

First form the regular bimodule maps
$$u_\eta:\mathcal D_\kappa\longrightarrow
\mathcal D_\kappa\otimes L_\eta\otimes V_\eta,\qquad
v_\eta:\mathcal D_\kappa\otimes V_\eta^*\longrightarrow
\mathcal D_\kappa\otimes L_\eta,$$
using coevaluation and evaluation. They are left action-algebroid maps and
right $\mathcal D_\kappa$-linear, with the right action on the first factor.
Let $E(V_\eta)=G\times^B V_\eta$. The map
$[g,v]\mapsto(gB,gv)$ identifies it with the trivial vector bundle
$X\times V_\eta$ carrying the diagonal infinitesimal action. A B-stable
filtration of $V_\eta$ with one-dimensional quotients therefore gives a
filtration of $E(V_\eta)$ whose line quotients are
$\mathcal O_X(\eta_j)$, where $\eta$ is the unique highest weight and every
other weight satisfies $\eta-\eta_j\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$ by [F1]–[F2].
On a local section of $G\to X$ from [F5], the PBW presentation of the regular
bimodules is the induced $U(\mathfrak g)$-module from the isotropy character
tensored with this filtered B-module. Its coevaluation quotients therefore
have central characters $\chi_{\kappa-\eta+\eta_j}$; the evaluation
quotients have central characters $\chi_{\kappa-\eta_j}$. This follows
because each quotient is the one-dimensional B-character $\eta_j$ before
induction, and the TDO parameter shifts by that character under [F4]; it is
not an appeal to a general tensor-character rule. The top-weight line in
$L_\eta\otimes E(V_\eta)$ is B-invariant and is the coevaluation image;
the quotient of $E(V_\eta)^*$ of weight $-\eta$ is the evaluation target.

For the coevaluation map, the distinguished top quotient has character
$\chi_\kappa$. If any other quotient had this character, W-invariance of
Harish–Chandra characters would give some $w\in W$ with
$\kappa-w\kappa=\eta-\eta_j\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$, contrary to [F3].
Hence the finite filtration has a unique generalized central-character
summand with character $\chi_\kappa$, and the coevaluation map identifies
$M$ with that summand.

For the evaluation map, the target has character $\chi_{\kappa-\eta}$.
If a source weight $\eta_j\ne\eta$ gave the same character, then for some
$w\in W$ one would have $\kappa-\eta_j=w(\kappa-\eta)$. Applying $w^{-1}$
and rearranging gives
$$\kappa-w^{-1}\kappa=\eta-w^{-1}\eta_j.$$
The right side lies in $Q_+$ because $w^{-1}\eta_j$ is again a weight of
$V_\eta$; if it is nonzero, [F3] forbids it, and if it is zero, regularity
in [F3] forces $w=1$, which then forces $\eta_j=\eta$, a contradiction.
Thus the target is exactly the unique generalized central-character summand
and the evaluation map splits onto it.

For a finite filtration with distinct central characters, the product of
their maximal ideals in the commutative center annihilates the filtered
module. Distinct maximal ideals are pairwise comaximal, so the Chinese
remainder theorem supplies orthogonal idempotent projectors in the quotient
by their product. For coevaluation, its image is the top-weight subbundle
and its associated quotient is the distinguished character $\chi_\kappa$;
for evaluation, the target is the distinguished lowest-weight quotient
$\chi_{\kappa-\eta}$. By steps 2.1 and 3.1 each distinguished character
occurs in exactly one filtration quotient. The maps therefore identify
their sources or targets with the corresponding generalized
central-character summands. The projectors are polynomials in central
elements on the induced modules, so they are left $U(\mathfrak g)$-linear,
B-equivariant, and commute with the right $U(\mathfrak g)$ action because
the center is central. On a torsor chart from [F5], a B-equivariant map of
the associated fiber modules extends as
$\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal O_U}\otimes\pi$, so it is $\mathcal O_U$-linear.
Its $U(\mathfrak g)$-linearity makes it commute with the left
action-algebroid generators; centrality makes it commute with right
multiplication on the regular TDO factor. Hence it is a bimodule map on the
chart. B-equivariance makes the local maps agree on overlaps. They thus
split $u_\eta$ and $v_\eta$ as
$\mathcal D_\kappa$-bimodule maps. For arbitrary $M$, tensor these splittings
over the right $\mathcal D_\kappa$ action with $M$. A split map remains split
under any tensor functor, so this gives the asserted maps for all
quasicoherent $M$, without a flatness assumption.

Since $\Gamma_\kappa$ is exact, its kernel $K$ is closed under
subobjects, quotients and extensions; hence $K$ is a Serre subcategory.
The functor $\Gamma_\kappa$ therefore descends to the Serre quotient.

Localization is right exact. For a short exact sequence
$0\to V'\to V\to V''\to0$ of $A_\kappa$-modules, applying localization
gives a right-exact sequence
$$\operatorname{Loc}V'\longrightarrow\operatorname{Loc}V
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Loc}V''\longrightarrow0.$$
Apply the exact functor $\Gamma_\kappa$ and use [F2]. The resulting sequence
is $0\to V'\to V\to V''\to0$. Therefore the kernel of
$\operatorname{Loc}V'\to\operatorname{Loc}V$ has zero global sections and
lies in $K$. Thus localization becomes exact after passage to the Serre
quotient.

The unit is an isomorphism by [F2], so it remains an isomorphism in the
quotient. For any $M$, the triangular identity in [F3] shows that applying
$\Gamma_\kappa$ to the counit
$\operatorname{Loc}_\kappa\Gamma_\kappa M\to M$ gives an isomorphism. By
exactness [F1], the kernel and cokernel of the counit lie in $K$; hence the
counit is an isomorphism in the quotient. The descended unit and counit
prove the claimed equivalence.

For an arbitrary $M$, let $E$ be the image of the counit
$\operatorname{Loc}_\kappa\Gamma M\to M$. By step 3.1 its cokernel has zero
global sections, so $E$ and $M$ define isomorphic objects of the Serre
quotient. The source is generated by its global sections, hence so is $E$.
Among the submodules of $E$ with zero global sections, take their sum $T$.
This is a set-indexed sum: a submodule sheaf is specified by a family of
subsets of the sets $E(U)$, one for each open $U\subseteq X$. The direct sum
of any such family is again a quasicoherent $\mathcal D_\kappa$-module, and
$\Gamma$ commutes with it by [F4]. Exactness of $\Gamma$ [F1] then gives
$\Gamma T=0$, so $T$ is the largest submodule of $E$ in $K$. The quotient
$E/T$ remains generated by global sections. If $S\subseteq E/T$ has
$\Gamma S=0$, its inverse image $P\subseteq E$ fits into
$0\to T\to P\to S\to0$; exactness [F1] gives $\Gamma P=0$, so $P\subseteq T$
by maximality and $S=0$. Thus $E/T$ is a representative of the same
quotient object, is generated by global sections, and has no nonzero
submodule in $K$. Conversely, every module with those two properties is by
definition such a representative.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from sheaf cohomology. Let $X$ be a
quasi-compact separated scheme ([[def-separated-morphism-schemes]]), let
$U_0,\dots,U_r$ be a finite affine open cover of $X$ and let $\mathcal F$ be a
quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module
([[def-quasi-coherent-module-scheme]]). Then every intersection of one or more
members of this cover is affine, and, writing $C^\bullet(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)$
for the ordered Čech cochain complex of the cover in the given order
([[def-cech-cochain-complex-open-cover]]), the canonical comparison map
$$\check H^q(\mathcal U,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow H^q(X,\mathcal F)$$
of the ordered Čech cohomology ([[def-cech-cohomology-open-cover]]) with sheaf
cohomology ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]) is an isomorphism
for every $q\ge0$. The empty scheme is included: its cover may have no
members or any finite number of empty members, and all cochain and cohomology
groups are zero, so the comparison is the unique map $0\to0$. An empty
index set is allowed in this case; $r=0$ gives a one-member cover.

[[lem-semisimple-minimal-parabolic-root-subgroup]] proves that it is closed,
contains $B$ and $U_{-\alpha}$, has
$\operatorname{Lie}P_\alpha=\mathfrak b\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$,
and satisfies $P_\alpha=B\sqcup Bn_\alpha B$ with $n_\alpha$ a Weyl
representative of $s_\alpha$. That lemma and
[[thm-minimal-parabolic-flag-projection-is-p1-bundle]] prove
$P_\alpha/B\cong\mathbb P^1$ and that $G/B\to G/P_\alpha$ is a Zariski

Every Verma module $M(\lambda)$, every quotient of it, and every finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module belongs to $\mathcal O$.

The **BGG category $\mathcal O$** is the full subcategory of left $U(\mathfrak g)$-modules $M$ satisfying all three conditions: $M$ is finitely generated; $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}M_\mu$ where $M_\mu=\{v:hv=\mu(h)v\text{ for all }h\in\mathfrak h\}$; and $U(\mathfrak n^+)v$ is finite dimensional for each $v\in M$. Its morphisms are all $\mathfrak g$-linear maps. The zero module is included, generated by the empty set.
